Felipe, Sarah Whitmore. A year ago I called you about a CFO role and you took the call in English for the first time. I want to put you in front of a board next month. Before I do, how would you describe where you are now?
Honestly? I'd say I've come a long way, though I'd stop short of calling it finished. Twelve months ago I could follow everything and produce almost nothing. Now I chair the quarterly call myself.
That is a real shift. What made the difference, do you think?

Repetition, mostly. It is muscle memory more than knowledge. The phrases arrive before I choose them. And I stopped apologizing for the pause. Now I fall back on one line: let me put that another way.
Some candidates tell me they are fluent and then freeze on the first difficult question. Where would you say your blind spot still is?
On a bad line, with three people talking at once. I hold my own in a meeting; a crowded call is still work. I would rather be candid about that than oversell it.
That answer is exactly why I am calling. One more thing: the board meets on the fourteenth. Will you be ready?
By the fourteenth I will have presented these numbers four times, so yes. And by then I will have been running this function in English for a full year. It will not be my first difficult room.
Good. I will send you the brief tonight. You have changed since that first call, haven't you?
I have. Same numbers, different voice.
I've come a long way, though I'd stop short of calling it finished.

Felipe, it is Sarah Whitmore from Hartley and Vance. I left you almost exactly this message a year ago, so forgive the symmetry. Back then I told you about a payments company looking for a finance leader, you called me back, and you took thirty minutes in English. I remember thinking at the time that the English was the smaller obstacle. It usually is. I am calling because the same client has come back to me, and this time the role is bigger and the conversation is with the board rather than the chief executive. Four people, one hour, and at least one question designed to see how you think when you have not prepared. Here is my honest advice, and it is the same advice I give every senior candidate. Do not walk in there trying to sound perfect. Walk in there able to say what you do not know, in a full sentence, without apologizing for it. That is what a board reads as seniority. Call me back this week. And Felipe, listen to the first message again if you still have it. You will not recognize the man who answered it.

I run language programs for companies, and at the end of every one I get the same question. What happens now. So here is the honest answer. Nothing collapses in a week, but a skill you stop using does fade, and the part that fades first is not grammar. It is speed. You will still understand everything. You will simply take a second longer to produce it, and that second is what other people mistake for your level. So protect the speed, not the vocabulary. Fifteen minutes of speaking out loud, three times a week, does more than two hours of reading. Record yourself once a month and keep the files, because progress at this stage is far too slow to feel and far too obvious to miss on two recordings six months apart. And find one room where you are the least fluent person present, and walk into it on purpose. Comfort is where a plateau begins. One last thing, and it is the one that matters. Do not measure yourself against a native speaker. They are not the benchmark and they never were. Measure yourself against the recording you made on your first day. That is the only comparison that has ever told anybody the truth.
